title: Refactor mono-observability bus: zero-copy span/log transfer and async ingest
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: The current observability stack fans out traces, logs, and metrics through multiple in-process queues and independent flush paths which increases allocation pressure, duplicates serialization work, and introduces tail latency under bursty workloads. Background: recent incidents (see ENG-742000) showed elevated p99 latencies and CPU spikes during model rollout churn. Goal: introduce a single lightweight in-process observability bus that centralizes enqueueing for spans/logs/metrics and enables zero-copy handoff to background async ingest workers. This reduces serialization duplication, shrinks heap allocations, and simplifies backpressure handling across telemetry types. Approach: (1) implement a mono-observability bus API with typed ring buffer segments for spans/logs/metrics, optimized for single-producer-many-consumer pattern, (2) integrate zero-copy transfer for span/log envelopes using shared memory slices and reference-counted buffers, (3) replace duplicated JSON/protobuf serializations with a unified compact wire encoder used by background ingest workers, (4) add adaptive batching policies per-tenant, and (5) provide feature flags and gradual rollout (canary then fleet) with safety fallbacks to the legacy fans-out path. Trade-offs: introduces a new shared memory abstraction that requires careful lifecycle handling and observability for the bus itself (we will add internal metrics). Risk: memory leaks if refcounts mishandled; plan to add crash-only sanity checks and canary with low-traffic tenants first. Coordination: will require upstream changes in runtime request path and minor changes to sidecar exporters. See links for design doc and PRs.
acceptance_criteria: Single in-process observability bus exists and is the default behind a feature flag
End-to-end path for traces and logs uses zero-copy handoff from request handler to async worker
p90 CPU consumption of observability hotpath reduced by >= 12% in synthetic bench
p99 telemetry flush latency reduced by >= 25% under 5x burst traffic in smoke tests
No increase in dropped telemetry events compared to baseline; backpressure metrics indicate healthy buffering
Graceful rollback path that reverts to legacy fans-out without loss during canary

comments: 2025-02-14: Kickoff — design sketched, agreed to prioritize zero-copy to minimize allocations. Decided to use ring buffer + reference-counted slices over mmap to support containerized deployments.

2025-02-15: Prototype succeeded: local bench shows 18% reduction in CPU on the hotpath and p99 telemetry enqueue latency dropped from ~35ms to ~20ms (synthetic). Prototype used a simplified compact encoder; need production-grade encoder and tests.
2025-02-17: Security reviewed the shared-slice approach; they requested explicit bounds checks and annotation of ownership in code comments. Security review ticked off with these mitigations.

2025-02-18: Opened initial PR for ring buffer and shared-slice types: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/9876 (WIP). Added benchmark harness in a separate PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/9889.

2025-02-19: Ran canary on internal staging with 10 tenants; observed steady-state CPU down ~14% and telemetry-driven tail latency improvement. Found an edge case where very large log messages (>256KB) caused refcount churn; added guard and fallback to copy path.

2025-02-20: Engineering review feedback: simplify public API to avoid leaking refcount manipulation to consumers. Plan to add helper wrappers and deprecate the old enqueue function after rollout completes. Scheduling follow-up: 2-day stabilization window post-canary before broader rollout.
